Sequelize Oracle SQLi: TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP quote-bypass payload in HTTP request AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP query strings / bodies carrying the CVE-2026-69240 payload shape — a parameter value beginning with TO_DATE( or TO_TIMESTAMP( followed by a quote break-out (||'', OR 1=1, --, UNION). This is the delivery vector that reaches Sequelize's vulnerable escape() path in the Oracle dialect. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC signature from the GHSA (`TO_DATE('0','Y')||'' OR 1=1--`): a param value opening with TO_DATE(/TO_TIMESTAMP( plus a break-out token. Legitimate query params never combine an Oracle date-cast function with `||''`/`OR 1=1`/`--`, making this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/sequelize/CVE-2026-69240/ • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-SEQUELIZE-2959225 • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-69240
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DAST/pentest tooling (sqlmap, Burp Scanner, Acunetix) firing SQLi payloads during authorized testing
  • An internal application that legitimately accepts Oracle TO_DATE(...) expressions as a search parameter (rare)
  • Security awareness / red-team exercises replaying known CVE payloads
  • WAF that decodes and logs the raw attack even though it blocked the request (still a true attempt, triage as such)
  • Copy/paste of Oracle SQL snippets into a free-text search field by a developer
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("<known-scanner-ip-placeholder>") // replace/remove if no sanctioned scanners; prefer excluding by scanner UserAgent when available
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request (SrcIP, UriPath, Query) and confirm the target app uses Sequelize with dialect=oracle and version < 6.37.4; check the HTTP status/response size to judge whether injection succeeded. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, add a virtual-patch rule dropping TO_DATE(/TO_TIMESTAMP( in user input, and prioritise upgrading Sequelize to >= 6.37.4. 3) Hunt: pivot on SrcIP for other endpoints/params hit, and cross-check the Oracle audit UC (below) for the same window to confirm the payload actually executed at the DB.
union
 (W3CIISLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=cIP, Host=Computer, Method=csMethod, UriPath=csUriStem, Query=csUriQuery, Status=tostring(scStatus)),
 (AppServiceHTTPLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=CIp, Host=CsHost, Method=CsMethod, UriPath=CsUriStem, Query=CsUriQuery, Status=tostring(ScStatus)),
 (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=SourceIP, Host=DestinationHostName, Method=RequestMethod, UriPath=RequestURL, Query=RequestURL, Status=tostring(EventOutcome))
| where Query has_any ("TO_DATE","TO_TIMESTAMP","to_date","to_timestamp")
| where Query matches regex @"(?i)(TO_DATE|TO_TIMESTAMP)\s*[\(%]"
| where Query has "||" or Query contains "%7C%7C" or Query matches regex @"(?i)\bor\b\s+1\s*=\s*1" or Query has "UNION" or Query contains "--"
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious @ali-impersonating npm packages installed into node_modules (Alibaba RAT cluster) AIDelivery High
Detects installation of the 18 named npm packages from the Socket-reported cross-platform RAT campaign that impersonate private @ali-scoped Alibaba packages. Fires on file writes into node_modules for any of the exact malicious package names, which is the earliest on-host signal of dependency-tree compromise. Rationale: Uses the complete verbatim package list from the article/Socket disclosure scoped to node_modules paths, so any hit is one of the exact malicious artifacts, not a generic supply-chain heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba • https://cybersecuritynews.com/npm-packages-cross-platform-rat/ • https://gbhackers.com/split-rat-components-across-npm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately named an internal package identically (e.g. a real private local-config-parser mirrored offline)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the packages in a sandbox
  • Package cache/mirror sync (Verdaccio/Nexus) replicating the names before removal
  • Old lockfile restore pulling a pre-March 2026 benign lib-mtop version
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm which package + version installed and whether the host has access to the real @ali-scoped registry (the campaign only fully activates in Alibaba-adjacent environments). Check the package.json dependency tree for smart-config-manager as the bridge. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the developer host, kill node processes, remove node_modules, and treat the machine as compromised. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same DeviceName for curl-fetched JS and the decoy aliyuncs/fcapp C2 callbacks; rotate any credentials, SSH keys, and cloud tokens present on the host from a clean machine.

npm/node loader spawning curl to fetch remote JavaScript from decoy Alibaba domains AIInstallation High
Detects the lib-mtop loader behaviour where a Node/npm process shells out to curl to download a hardcoded remote JavaScript payload that is then executed via require(). Scopes to curl children of node/npm whose command line references the campaign's aliyuncs/fcapp/ai-app.pub decoy hosts. Rationale: Pairs the article's stated loader mechanic (node -> curl -> require) with the specific C2 host substrings, giving a parent-child + command-line triple that no legitimate npm workflow produces. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba • https://cybersecuritynews.com/npm-packages-cross-platform-rat/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build script legitimately using curl to pull a tarball from a real aliyuncs.com OSS bucket (verify exact subdomain against IOC list)
  • Node-based CI tooling that fetches assets via curl during install
  • Developer manually testing curl from an npm run-script
  • Internal package that vendors curl-based postinstall fetch of internal artifacts
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","github.com","githubusercontent.com"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the full curl URL from the command line and compare the host against the IOC set (aone-cli-next.oss-cn-beijing.aliyuncs.com and siblings); benign OSS buckets differ in subdomain. Step 2 (contain): Kill the node and curl processes, block the resolved host at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Look for the downloaded JS being require()'d, any vm-module secondary payload, and follow-on OS-specific persistence (UC4/UC5) on the same DeviceName.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","curl")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("aliyuncs.com","fcapp.run","ai-app.pub")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "curl"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","pnpm","yarn")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("aliyuncs.com","fcapp.run","ai-app.pub")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network callback to decoy Alibaba OSS / Aliyun Function Compute RAT C2 hosts AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS/network egress to the campaign's payload-staging and C2 domains that masquerade as Alibaba OSS and Aliyun Function Compute endpoints to blend into legitimate Alibaba traffic. These full hostnames are hard IOCs from the article's pre-extracted set. Rationale: These are fully-qualified IOC hostnames unique to the campaign; the aone-* aliyuncs subdomains are attacker-controlled buckets distinct from generic *.aliyuncs.com, so exact-match keeps FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba • https://gbhackers.com/split-rat-components-across-npm/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox or IOC-validation tooling resolving the hosts on purpose
  • Proxy/DNS security appliance pre-resolving submitted URLs for categorization
  • An analyst manually curling the IOC during investigation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process (node/curl vs browser) and whether the resolution succeeded and returned data. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block the domains org-wide, isolate the resolving host, and snapshot for forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with UC1/UC2 on the same host, review outbound bytes to the resolved IP for secondary-payload download, and sweep all dev hosts' DNS logs for the same five hosts.

Linux RAT payload dropped to /tmp then self-deleted after in-memory load AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Linux branch of the RAT that downloads a binary to /tmp, runs it as a detached process, and deletes the file from disk once loaded into memory. Correlates a short-lived /tmp file create+delete pair on the same host driven by a download/interpreter process. Rationale: Encodes the article's exact Linux TTP (download to /tmp, detached exec, delete-after-load) as a create+delete correlation restricted to download/interpreter processes, which is the defining anti-forensic behaviour of this branch. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package managers extracting to /tmp and cleaning up (apt, pip build temp dirs)
  • Shell scripts using mktemp for transient work files
  • Compilers/CI writing and removing intermediate objects in /tmp
  • Browser or updater temp-download-then-move operations
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("mktemp","apt","dpkg","pip"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Recover the initiating command line and the /tmp filename; check whether the detached process is still resident (ps/lsof by inode) despite the on-disk file being gone. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, capture memory of the orphaned/detached process before reboot, and block associated C2. Step 3 (hunt): Tie back to UC1/UC3 for the npm install and aliyuncs download that seeded it, and check for lateral-movement attempts described as a final-payload capability.
let Created = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","node","bash","sh")
| project CreateTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileDeleted"
| where FolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
| project DeleteTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath
| join kind=inner Created on DeviceName, FolderPath
| where DeleteTime between (CreateTime .. CreateTime + 5m)
| project DeviceName, FolderPath, CreateTime, DeleteTime, SecondsAlive=datetime_diff('second', DeleteTime, CreateTime), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by CreateTime desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/tmp/"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileDeleted")
| summarize Events=make_set(EventType), CreateTime=minif(TimeGenerated, EventType=="FileCreated"), DeleteTime=maxif(TimeGenerated, EventType=="FileDeleted"), Proc=any(ActingProcessName) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath
| where array_length(Events)==2 and DeleteTime > CreateTime and datetime_diff('minute', DeleteTime, CreateTime) <= 5
| where Proc has_any ("curl","wget","node","bash","sh")
| order by CreateTime desc
source:linux.auditd @process.name:(curl OR wget OR node) @process.command_line:(*\/tmp\/*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/^\/tmp\// ContextImageFileName=/(curl|wget|node|bash|sh)$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=FileDeleted TargetFileName=/^\/tmp\//}, field=[aid, TargetFileName], include=[TargetFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

macOS RAT persistence via ~/.zshrc injection and 10-minute LaunchAgent AIInstallation Medium
Detects the macOS branch of the RAT that persists by inserting a background script into ~/.zshrc and installing a LaunchAgent plist. Scopes file writes to those two persistence locations when driven by node/npm/curl/osascript rather than an interactive shell editor. Rationale: Combines the two named macOS persistence locations from the article with a non-interactive writer constraint (node/npm/curl/osascript), which cleanly separates the malware's scripted write from a developer editing their own shell profile. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba
ATT&CKT1546.004 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dotfile managers (chezmoi, yadm) or Homebrew post-install writing to .zshrc
  • Legitimate app installers dropping their own LaunchAgent plist
  • Developer tooling (nvm, pyenv) appending shell-init lines to .zshrc
  • IDE/setup scripts registering a LaunchAgent for background services
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chezmoi","yadm","brew","nvm","pyenv"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the injected .zshrc line / LaunchAgent plist ProgramArguments and check the referenced binary or URL against the campaign IOCs (aliyuncs/fcapp hosts). Note the LaunchAgent's 10-minute StartInterval as a strong tell. Step 2 (contain): Remove the persistence entries, unload the LaunchAgent, isolate the host, kill resident RAT processes. Step 3 (hunt): Check for injection into DingTalk/Wukong/Qoder collaboration apps, correlate to UC1's npm install, and rotate developer credentials from a clean machine.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName == ".zshrc" or FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","curl","osascript")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName == ".zshrc" or TargetFilePath contains "/Library/LaunchAgents/"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","curl","osascript")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

mrmustard PyPI stealer exfil to metrics.femboy.energy / webhook.site AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the secondary campaign in the article: the trojanized mrmustard 0.7.4 PyPI package whose _check_tf_compatibility() stealer harvests SSH keys, AWS creds and Kubernetes configs and beacons to metrics.femboy.energy/v1/collect (XOR key tf_compat_v2), with CI publishing-secret exfil to a webhook.site URL. Fires on egress to those hosts. Rationale: metrics.femboy.energy/v1/collect is the confirmed C2 (StepSecurity/SafeDep, decoded from XOR key tf_compat_v2) and the webhook.site GUID is the exact CI-secret exfil sink named in the article; both are hard IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-pypi-mrmustard-0-7-4-credential-stealer • https://safedep.io/mrmustard-malicious-pypi-package/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using webhook.site for their own webhook testing (validate the exact GUID path)
  • Security research/detonation of mrmustard in a sandbox
  • IOC-validation curling the C2
  • webhook.site used by an unrelated internal integration test
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process (python importing mrmustard is the tell) and whether the destination is the exact webhook.site GUID vs generic testing. Confirm mrmustard 0.7.4 is installed (pip show). Step 2 (contain): Block femboy.energy and the webhook.site URL, isolate the host, and immediately treat SSH keys, AWS credentials, Kubernetes configs, and any CI publishing tokens on that host as compromised — rotate from a clean machine. Step 3 (hunt): Remove the three persistence mechanisms that survive uninstall, downgrade mrmustard, and audit CI runners for the self-hosted-runner probing / secret theft described in the report.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("metrics.femboy.energy","webhook.site/710babde-6ace-47fe-83f4-9688e6548df9")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| where DnsQuery has "femboy.energy" or DnsQuery == "webhook.site"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

Google Password Manager Attacks Could Let Malware Hijack Passkey-Protected Accounts

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 9 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Malware running as an ordinary user on a Windows machine can sign into a victim's passkey-protected accounts without a fingerprint, a PIN, or anything at all appearing on the victim's screen. Unit 42 detailed three attack paths against Chrome's Google Password Manager cloud authenticator, which it calls Pass-ta-key, Silver Pass-ta-key and Golden Pass-ta-key; the strongest targets the master key

ATT&CKT1190 T1566 T1566.002
Domainswebauthm.io
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Command line referencing Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB path
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Google Password Manager Attacks Could Let Malware Hijack Passkey-Protected Accou
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Chrome process reading chrome.exe memory to steal passkey Security Domain Secret (Golden Pass-ta-key) · [LLM] Non-Chrome process tampering with Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB
Non-Chrome process reading chrome.exe memory to steal passkey Security Domain Secret (Golden Pass-ta-key) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a non-browser process opening a read handle into chrome.exe address space to scrape the 32-byte Security Domain Secret (SDS) while it sits in plaintext during passkey re-enrollment. Unit 42's Golden Pass-ta-key path reads the SDS out of Chrome process memory to decrypt all synced passkey private keys, so any non-Chrome, non-AV process reading Chrome memory is high-signal. Rationale: Uses the exact Golden Pass-ta-key behaviour from the Unit 42 report (SDS read from chrome.exe process memory) via Defender's raw OpenProcessApiCall/ReadProcessMemoryApiCall telemetry and Sysmon EID 10, scoping TargetImage=chrome.exe and excluding Chrome's own processes and AV. Datadog/Falcon left blank because neither the provided Sysmon EID subset nor an FDR process-access simpleName cleanly expresses cross-process read handles. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/google-authenticators-hidden-passkey-architecture/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Defender (MsMpEng.exe) scanning Chrome memory
  • Endpoint DLP / EDR agents inspecting browser processes
  • Task Manager or Process Explorer opened by an admin to inspect Chrome
  • Crash-reporting tools (crashpad_handler) reading Chrome on a hang
  • Browser performance/telemetry agents with legitimate read access
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","taskmgr.exe","procexp64.exe","procexp.exe","MpDefenderCoreService.exe","SenseIR.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Google\Chrome\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256 and folder path of the reader; confirm it is not AV/DLP/crashpad and is not signed by Google. Check GrantedAccess mask for PROCESS_VM_READ and whether the process was newly written to disk. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process, and force a Google account passkey/SDS re-enrollment and PIN change for the signed-in user (assume all synced passkeys are compromised). 3) Hunt: pivot on the reader's SHA256 across the fleet, check for prior file access to passkey_enclave_state / Sync Data LevelDB, and review the affected Google account for anomalous passkey assertions or new device enrollments.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("OpenProcessApiCall", "ReadProcessMemoryApiCall")
| where FileName =~ "chrome.exe"                       // target process being read = Chrome
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe"      // Chrome's own multi-process reads are legit
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Google\Chrome\"   // exclude crashpad_handler / updater
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","taskmgr.exe","procexp64.exe","procexp.exe","csrss.exe","wininit.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcess = FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 10   // ProcessAccess
| where EventData has "chrome.exe"                                // TargetImage
| where EventData has_any ("0x1010","0x1410","0x1438","0x143a","0x1fffff","0x0010")  // GrantedAccess incl PROCESS_VM_READ
| where EventData !has @"\Google\Chrome\"                        // exclude Chrome/updater as the source
| where EventData !has "MsMpEng.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-Chrome process tampering with Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a non-Chrome process writing, copying, renaming, or deleting Chrome's passkey device-key store (passkey_enclave_state) or the synced-credential LevelDB. Copy-out feeds offline SDS/passkey recovery; deletion forces the device re-enrollment window that Silver/Golden Pass-ta-key abuse to register an attacker UV key. Rationale: Anchored on the exact artifacts named in the Unit 42 report — passkey_enclave_state (wrapped device key + SDS + PIN) and the Sync Data\LevelDB WebauthnCredentialSpecifics store — with any non-Chrome, non-Google-signed writer/deleter surfaced. Deletion maps to the forced re-enrollment window abused by Silver/Golden; copy-out maps to offline recovery. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1556
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OneDrive / enterprise backup agents syncing the Chrome profile folder
  • Chrome profile migration or roaming-profile tooling
  • Antivirus quarantine touching files under User Data
  • Admin manually deleting a corrupt Chrome profile to fix sync
  • Endpoint management agents wiping browser data on offboarding
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MpDefenderCoreService.exe","backup.exe","cbsystray.exe") and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "Google LLC"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is not Google-signed, OneDrive, or backup software; note ActionType (Delete vs Create/Modify) and whether a copy of passkey_enclave_state / LevelDB landed outside the profile. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill/quarantine the process, and treat the user's synced passkeys as compromised — trigger passkey re-enrollment and PIN rotation on the Google account. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (chrome.exe memory reads) on the same host, search for exfil of the copied store over the network, and review the Google account for new device enrollments or attacker-registered UV keys.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state"
      or (FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" and FolderPath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "Google LLC"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Google\Chrome\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","backup.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state"
      or (TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" and TargetFilePath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where ActingProcessName !has @"\chrome.exe"
| where ActingProcessName !has @"\Google\Chrome\"
| where ActingProcessName !has @"\OneDrive.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Command line referencing Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB path AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts LOLBins/scripts (cmd, powershell, esentutl, robocopy, xcopy) invoked with Chrome's passkey store path on the command line — the tooling-based variant of Pass-ta-key local reconnaissance that enumerates relying parties, usernames and encrypted passkey material. Rationale: Targets the article's stated local-recon step (reading credential IDs, relying parties and usernames from Sync Data\LevelDB) plus the passkey_enclave_state path from the Unit 42 report, catching the copy/enumeration variant that uses native tooling rather than in-process API reads. Lower confidence/hunting tier because sophisticated malware reads via API and leaves nothing on the command line. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
ATT&CKT1217 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Support/IT scripts backing up or clearing a Chrome profile
  • Forensic/DFIR triage collection referencing the LevelDB path
  • Browser-data migration utilities
  • Developer debugging Chrome sync with the path in a script
  • Security tooling that inventories browser credential stores
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and not (AccountName has_any ("svc-dfir","admin-backup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the full command line and parent process — is this an admin/DFIR script, a migration tool, or an unexpected LOLBin (esentutl/robocopy/powershell) run by a standard user? Check the executing account and host role. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host and kill the process; preserve any output/copy of the passkey store for IR and rotate the affected Google account passkeys. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent process and user to UC1/UC2 (chrome memory reads and file tamper), check for archive/exfil of the collected data, and sweep the fleet for the same command-line pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("passkey_enclave_state", @"Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data" or ProcessCommandLine has "passkey_enclave_state"
| where FileName !~ "chrome.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("passkey_enclave_state", @"Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "passkey_enclave_state"
| where TargetProcessName !has @"\chrome.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo

SonicWall SMA 1000 /wsproxy SSRF exploitation (CVE-2026-15409, UTA0533/INC) AIExploitation High
Hunts UTA0533/INC-Ransomware exploitation of the SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF flaw CVE-2026-15409 via crafted /wsproxy requests that pivot the appliance to internal SSH/services. Article-specific because it keys on the exact exploit query-string (serviceType=SSH, host=0.0.0.0, bmID=-3389) and the 'SMA Connect Agent' user-agent Volexity observed. Rationale: Uses Volexity's exact CVE-2026-15409 exploit signature (GET /wsproxy?bmID=-3389&serviceType=SSH&host=0.0.0.0) plus the 'SMA Connect Agent' user-agent. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: the SMA 1000 is a Linux appliance whose inbound HTTP is only visible in appliance/CEF web logs, not endpoint EDR or AWS/Datadog standard sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-sma1000-flaws-exploited-as-zero-days-to-push-custom-malware/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/21/sonicwall-sma-zero-days-exploited-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SonicWall SMA Connect Agent client establishing bookmark/proxy sessions to authorized hosts
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing /wsproxy during a scheduled scan window
  • SonicWall support/diagnostics tooling reproducing wsproxy calls
  • Authorized red-team/pentest engagement against the appliance
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication =~ "SMA Connect Agent" and RequestURL !has "host=0.0.0.0" and RequestURL !has "bmID=-3389")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all /wsproxy hits from the SourceIP; confirm whether serviceType/host/port point at internal RFC1918 targets (real exploitation) vs authorized bookmark hosts. Check if SourceIP is an ExpressVPN/Mullvad exit (UTA0533 pattern). 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the perimeter, force the SMA 1000 to the mid-July 2026 patched firmware, and isolate the appliance from the internal LAN pending review. 3) Hunt: search the same appliance for the ORANGETAIL/Suo5 gating UA (UC2), for deploy_new.py/xzfind (UC3), and for tcpdump LDAP capture (UC4); rotate all VPN credentials and TOTP MFA seeds.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has "SonicWall" or DeviceProduct has "SMA"
| where (RequestURL has "/wsproxy" and (RequestURL has "serviceType=SSH" or RequestURL has "host=0.0.0.0" or RequestURL has "bmID=-3389")) or RequestClientApplication =~ "SMA Connect Agent"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA ORANGETAIL/Suo5 web-shell access via hardcoded gating user-agent AIInstallation High
Detects requests to the ORANGETAIL Java web shell and Suo5 proxy planted on SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances, which are gated behind a hardcoded, fabricated user-agent (Mozilla/6.0 ... Chrome/149.0.0.1) and reached through nginx-rewritten error.jsp routes. Article/Volexity-specific: 'Mozilla/6.0' and 'Chrome/149.0.0.1' are non-existent versions unique to this campaign. Rationale: Keys on the campaign-unique gating user-agent (Mozilla/6.0 with Chrome/149.0.0.1 - both fabricated versions) plus the nginx-rewritten error.jsp routes Volexity documented for ORANGETAIL/Suo5. The UA alone is near-zero-FP because those version tokens do not exist in real browsers. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-exploit-sonicwall-sma-zero-days-to-gain-root-access/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1090
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users hitting /workplace/error.jsp or errorDialog.jsp during normal SMA portal error handling (UA-only rule avoids this)
  • Security scanners deliberately spoofing malformed user-agents against the portal
  • Synthetic uptime/monitoring probes configured with a custom UA string
  • Browser QA testing with an overridden user-agent
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting SourceIP and whether the fabricated UA appears alongside error.jsp/errorDialog.jsp access; a match on the UA is effectively confirmation of web-shell interaction. 2) Contain: isolate the SMA 1000 from the LAN, block the SourceIP, and image the appliance before rebuild - do not just patch, the web shell is JVM-injected. 3) Hunt: inspect /var/lib/unit/conf.json for the 127.0.0.1:8085 proxy route, look for deploy_new.py and the /tmp/agent_wp8.jar & agent_wp9.jar drops (UC3), and review internal auth for lateral movement tunneled via Suo5.

| where DeviceVendor has "SonicWall" or DeviceProduct has "SMA"
| where (RequestClientApplication has "Mozilla/6.0" and RequestClientApplication has "Chrome/149.0.0.1")
    or RequestURL has_any ("/__api__/login","/__api__/logout","/workplace/error.jsp","/workplace/dialogs/errorDialog.jsp")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

KNUCKLEBALL loader, JAR payload drops & init.d persistence on SonicWall SMA AIInstallation High
Hunts the KNUCKLEBALL Python loader (deploy_new.py in the python3.11 site-packages dir), its two staged JARs (agent_wp8.jar=Suo5, agent_wp9.jar=ORANGETAIL), the xzfind ROOTRUN privesc binary, and the /etc/init.d/workplace persistence edit on compromised SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances. Entirely article/Volexity-specific file artifacts. Rationale: Uses Volexity's exact malware paths (deploy_new.py in site-packages, /tmp/agent_wp8.jar & agent_wp9.jar, /usr/bin/xzfind ROOTRUN, /tmp/1234.sh) plus the 'running hotfix removal for:../' path-traversal log string. SHA256s (8c470301..., ea9154e3..., 1e1e68bb..., 81a9af38...) match these files. Falcon/Defender empty: the appliance is not an EDR-managed host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://socradar.io/blog/sonicwall-sma-knuckleball-malware/
ATT&CKT1037.004 T1059.006 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SonicWall firmware/hotfix updates writing to site-packages or modifying /etc/init.d/workplace
  • Vendor support scripts staged under /tmp during a diagnostics session
  • Admin-authored maintenance scripts named similarly in /tmp
  • Backup/AV agents reading (not writing) these paths
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash any deploy_new.py / xzfind / *.jar present and compare to the Volexity SHA256s (deploy_new.py=8c470301..., xzfind=81a9af38..., agent_wp9.jar/ORANGETAIL=ea9154e3..., agent_wp8.jar/Suo5=1e1e68bb...). 2) Contain: power-isolate and rebuild the appliance from clean firmware - JVM-injected payloads survive simple file deletion; remove the deploy_new.py line from /etc/init.d/workplace. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC4 (tcpdump LDAP capture), review /var/lib/unit/conf.json for the 8085 proxy route, and rotate credentials/TOTP seeds harvested from the appliance.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("deploy_new.py","/tmp/agent_wp8.jar","/tmp/agent_wp9.jar","/usr/bin/xzfind","/tmp/1234.sh","running hotfix removal for:../")

| sort by TimeGenerated desc

tcpdump LDAP credential sniffing on SonicWall SMA appliance AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the UTA0533 credential-harvesting step where tcpdump is run on a compromised SonicWall SMA appliance to capture cleartext LDAP (TCP 389) authentication traffic, driven by the /var/tmp/lib.sh helper. Article/Volexity-specific credential-access behaviour on the appliance itself. Rationale: Uses Volexity's documented credential-harvesting command (tcpdump on TCP 389 for cleartext LDAP) and the /var/tmp/lib.sh storage helper. Medium confidence/FP because admins do legitimately run tcpdump - the LDAP-389 + /var/tmp/lib.sh combination is the discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.securityweek.com/sonicwall-zero-days-exploited-to-deliver-custom-malware-for-weeks-before-patch/

Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/session that launched tcpdump and whether a capture file was written under /var/tmp; correlate the timestamp to any UC1/UC2 exploitation hit. 2) Contain: kill the tcpdump process, isolate the appliance, and treat all LDAP/AD credentials that authenticated through it as compromised. 3) Hunt: rotate the exposed directory-service credentials and TOTP MFA seeds immediately, then hunt for use of those creds via internal auth logs and for Suo5-tunneled lateral movement.

INC Ransomware encryption: .inc mass file writes and INC-README notes AIActions on Objectives High
Detects INC Ransomware's on-host impact stage on internal Windows endpoints reached via the SonicWall SMA foothold: high-volume file writes/renames to the .inc extension plus creation of INC-README.txt / INC-README.html ransom notes. Enriched from SentinelOne/Huntress INC artifacts since the article names the actor but not the note/extension. Rationale: Article names INC Ransomware as the dominant actor; SentinelOne and Huntress confirm INC writes INC-README.txt/.html notes and appends the .inc extension. The 5-minute >100-file threshold OR any ransom-note write is the mass-encryption discriminator and separates it from benign .inc include files. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/anthology/inc-ransom/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/investigating-new-inc-ransom-group-activity • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1486 T1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer machines mass-writing .inc PHP/ASP/CAD include files during a build (excluded by dev-tool filter + threshold)
  • Backup or archival software touching many files with an .inc-suffixed temp name
  • Legacy applications that legitimately use .inc as a data extension
  • Bulk file-server migration jobs generating high write counts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msbuild.exe","devenv.exe","php.exe","cmake.exe","node.exe") or Notes > 0
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged DeviceName confirm the InitiatingProcess writing .inc files is not a known dev/build tool and that INC-README.txt/.html notes exist; check InitiatingProcessSHA256 against INC IOCs. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network immediately, suspend the offending process, and disable the associated account; snapshot for forensics before any reboot. 3) Hunt: trace the intrusion back to the SMA 1000 (UC1-UC4), check for VSS deletion/backup tampering, and sweep all hosts reachable via the compromised VPN for the same .inc/INC-README pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".inc" or FileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")
| summarize FileCount = count(), Notes = countif(FileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 5), Folders = dcount(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FileCount > 100 or Notes > 0
| sort by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "inc" or TargetFileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")
| summarize FileCount = count(), Notes = countif(TargetFileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html")), SampleFiles = make_set(TargetFileName, 5) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FileCount > 100 or Notes > 0
| sort by FileCount desc

UTA0533/INC SonicWall exploitation source-IP network IOCs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects endpoint or network communication with the four Volexity-confirmed UTA0533 exploitation/web-shell source IPs (108.205.8.173, 147.45.51.19, 150.241.210.53, 81.19.140.217) used against SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances. Surfaces both inbound appliance interaction and any Suo5-tunneled traffic seen by internal hosts. Rationale: Uses only the four non-VPN sample IPs Volexity published (the campaign also used 200+ ExpressVPN/Mullvad exits, which would be too noisy to ship). Dropped helprans.com and four other article-only IPs (202.8.105.201, 217.77.15.99, 42.200.172.14, 89.117.20.1) as single-source per corroboration rules. Medium confidence because IPs can be reassigned. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195626/hacking/volexity-uncovers-zero-day-campaign-targeting-sonicwall-vpn-appliances.html

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign users behind a recycled datacenter/VPN IP that was previously attacker-controlled
  • Threat-intel or ASM scanning services legitimately probing your perimeter from a listed IP
  • IP reassigned by the hosting provider to a new tenant after the campaign
  • Internal proxy egressing many users' traffic through one of these addresses
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine direction - inbound to the SMA 1000 (exploitation source) vs an internal host reaching out (possible tunneled C2); pull the process (InitiatingProcessFileName) on any internal hit. 2) Contain: block all four IPs at the perimeter and, for any internal host that contacted them, isolate and inspect for web-shell/Suo5 activity. 3) Hunt: correlate the IP timestamps with UC1/UC2 web-log hits, verify appliance patch level, and rotate credentials/TOTP seeds if the appliance interacted with these IPs.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] LockBit payload execution via PsExec service (PsExecSvc.exe → 1.exe/LBB.exe) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
RDP re-enable + EDR/Defender disable batch script (LockBit intrusion) AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-access batch script observed in the leaked-LockBit-builder case that enabled RDP by setting fDenyTSConnections to 0 and disabled endpoint defenses before ransomware deployment. Anchors on the exact registry value/data pair the article's script wrote. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim registry write from the article's disable-defenses batch script (HKLM\...\Control\Terminal Server \ fDenyTSConnections = 0) which turns RDP on; pairs it with reg.exe execution to keep fidelity high. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/lockbit-3-0-based-custom-targeted-ransomware/112375/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lockbit-ransomware-builder-leaked-online-by-angry-developer/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately enabling RDP on a new server build via a provisioning script
  • GPO/DSC/Intune configuration baseline that manages fDenyTSConnections
  • MSP onboarding automation that turns on RDP for remote management
  • Server 2016 role-setup wizards that toggle Remote Desktop
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","omadmclient.exe","gpscript.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating account and parent process of the reg.exe/registry write; confirm whether the same host also saw EDR/Defender service stops in the surrounding minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable the account used to write the value, and re-set fDenyTSConnections to 1 if the change was unauthorized. 3) Hunt: pivot on the account across DeviceLogonEvents for RDP (LogonType 10) and search for PsExecSvc.exe/named ransomware payloads (1.exe, LBB.exe) and Defender-tamper events fleet-wide.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Terminal Server"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "fDenyTSConnections"
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("SystemSettings.exe","ServerManager.exe","mmc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe"
| where CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections" and CommandLine has_any ("/d 0","/d 0x0")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
