LockBit payload execution via PsExec service (PsExecSvc.exe → 1.exe/LBB.exe) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the manual lateral deployment of the custom LockBit build from the leaked builder: the sample was configured without psexec_netspread, so operators used PsExec (PsExecSvc.exe) to remotely launch ransomware binaries named 1.EXE and LBB.exe. Targets the impact/deployment step, not generic PsExec admin use. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim payload names (1.EXE, LBB.exe) and the PsExecSvc.exe service the operators relied on for manual spread after building a variant without psexec_netspread; combining parent + payload names keeps the otherwise-generic 1.exe fidelity acceptable. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/lockbit-3-0-based-custom-targeted-ransomware/112375/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/dragonforce-ransomware
ATT&CKT1486 T1569.002 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sysadmin using Sysinternals PsExec for remote software rollout (PsExecSvc.exe as parent)
  • Automation/RMM that names a tool 1.exe in a temp build path
  • Software packaging test binaries transiently named 1.exe
  • Remote patch scripts pushed via PsExec across a fleet
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\SCCM\\","\\ccmcache\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the SHA256 and full path of the spawned binary and the source host driving PsExecSvc.exe; check for mass DeviceFileEvents FileRenamed/FileModified bursts on the same device. 2) Contain: network-isolate affected hosts, block the payload hash, and disable the deploying account. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host where PsExecSvc.exe appeared (USN Journal .KEY artifacts corroborate historic spread), look for kill_defender/Defender-uninstall events and wallpaper/registry changes indicative of LockBit encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "PsExecSvc.exe"
    or FileName in~ ("1.exe","LBB.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName endswith "\\PsExecSvc.exe")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\1.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\LBB.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Potato privilege-escalation tooling (GodPotato / SweetPotato / BadPotato) AIExploitation High
Hunts the SeImpersonate token-abuse tools the article attributes to the observed privilege-escalation activity in these intrusions. Anchors on the exact tool family names used to move from a service/valid account to SYSTEM. Rationale: Anchors on the three Potato variant names the article explicitly attributes to privilege escalation (GodPotato, SweetPotato, BadPotato); these are offensive-only tool names, so name/cmdline matches are high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/incidents-at-brazilian-educational-institutions/120803/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

AnyDesk silent/unattended install used for DragonForce access AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the attacker-driven AnyDesk deployment the article ties to DragonForce (Case 02): AnyDesk installed and configured for unattended access to give operators remote control before ransomware. Anchors on the unattended-install command-line flags rather than mere presence of AnyDesk. Rationale: Anchors on AnyDesk (named in Case 02 as the DragonForce remote-access vector) combined with unattended-install flags that legitimate interactive users rarely pass, corroborated by DragonForce write-ups documenting silent AnyDesk installs for persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/dragonforce-ransomware-attack/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/dragonforce-ransomware
ATT&CKT1219 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk legitimately deploying AnyDesk unattended via GPO/RMM
  • MSP standardizing on AnyDesk for remote support with --start-with-win
  • User self-installing AnyDesk from a legit MSI that passes --silent
  • Vendor support session where AnyDesk is provisioned with a set password
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("AnyDesk.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the installing account and parent process (deployment tool vs. email client vs. script) and whether AnyDesk is a sanctioned tool for this host/OU. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill AnyDesk, and rotate credentials; capture the AnyDesk ID/anydesk.trace for the incoming operator IP. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents for AnyDesk relay traffic (boot.net.anydesk.com / *.relay), then look for DragonForce indicators — PsExec spread, mass encryption, ransom notes — across hosts that ran AnyDesk in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "AnyDesk.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--install","--silent","--start-with-win","--set-password","--get-id")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\AnyDesk.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--install","--silent","--start-with-win","--set-password")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

SecurityEvent

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chinese Threat Actor Uses Leaked DarkSword Kit to Deploy GHOSTBLADE on iOS

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 9 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An unknown Chinese-speaking threat actor has been observed running a campaign targeting Apple iOS devices by leveraging a publicly leaked version of the DarkSword exploit kit. Attack surface management platform Censys said it identified the threat actor running more than 100 web properties, most of which are fake Amazon Web Services (AWS) sign-in pages on a domain that also hosts the exploit

ATT&CKT1190 T1566 T1566.002
Domainst.me/YATA0000
IPs38.181.52.95 103.106.190.217 38.22.89.117 103.97.128.67 162.4.136.30 223.26.63.56 151.243.126.191 107.175.49.181 103.238.129.112 103.226.155.200 103.226.155.201 202.8.120.249 93.152.221.37

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Browser web session to fake AWS-console / Apple ID DarkSword watering-hole hosts · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Egress to DarkSword/GHOSTBLADE exploit-panel and C2 infrastructure IPs · [LLM] Proxy hunt for DarkSword operator Telegram contact channel t.me/YATA0000 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Egress to DarkSword/GHOSTBLADE exploit-panel and C2 infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control High
Alerts when any managed host (Windows/macOS endpoint, or an iOS/BYOD device traversing a corporate firewall or proxy) connects to the 13 Censys-identified DarkSword Admin, Decode Dashboard, and C2 Control Panel IPs that also host the GHOSTBLADE credential-exfil endpoints. This is the only honest way to surface an iOS DarkSword compromise on non-iOS telemetry — the implant's file/keychain/iCloud exfil sweep transits these hosts. Rationale: Uses the 13 concrete C2/exploit-panel IPs from the Censys/THN analysis (panels on :8888 and :3000, Decode Dashboard, C2 Control Panel co-hosting the Apple ID decoy, and the Frankfurt open-directory tooling host). Cross-checked against GTIG's DarkSword write-up confirming the kit/GHOSTBLADE family; IPs themselves trace to the single Censys source so keep at alerting-with-triage. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/darksword-ios-exploit-chain • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-darksword-ios-exploit-used-in-infostealer-attack-on-iphones/ • https://iverify.io/blog/darksword-ios-exploit-kit-explained
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Your own attack-surface/TI scanners (Censys, Shodan, RiskIQ agents) beaconing the same hosting IPs from a corporate egress range
  • Automated IOC-enrichment/sandbox tooling auto-resolving these indicators from a SOAR host
  • A shared-hosting IP being re-assigned to a benign tenant after takedown (validate the port and whether the panel front-end still responds)
  • Threat-intel researchers on the network manually browsing the exposed panels
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("censys-scanner.exe","nmap.exe","masscan.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\SOAR\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and whether it is a Windows/macOS endpoint or an iOS/BYOD device on corp WiFi; check the initiating process and destination port (8888/3000 = admin panel access, 80/443 = phishing-page/exploit delivery). 2) Contain: block all 13 IPs at the firewall/proxy, isolate the source device; for a suspected iOS victim, force an Apple ID password reset and revoke iCloud/keychain sessions (GHOSTBLADE dumps keychain, iCloud, and Wi-Fi creds). 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP across DNS/proxy for the other 12 IPs and the t.me/YATA0000 operator channel, and review AAD/Apple ID sign-ins from anomalous geographies following the connection.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (DarkSwordIPs)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Attempts=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc

| order by LastSeen desc

Browser web session to fake AWS-console / Apple ID DarkSword watering-hole hosts AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces a corporate browser navigating to the DarkSword-operator IPs that serve fake AWS sign-in and Apple ID credential-harvesting pages hosting the malicious iframe that fires the exploit chain. Targets the initial-access step where an AWS admin or user is lured to the watering hole from a managed desktop before any iOS payload runs. Rationale: Article states the chain begins when a victim reaches an AWS-console impersonation subdomain or Apple ID sign-in page hosting the malicious iframe; scopes the delivery-side IPs (Singapore multi-front-end 38.181.52.95, Apple ID decoy 103.106.190.217, the six :8888/:3000 exploit panels) to browser-initiated sessions, distinguishing a lured user from generic egress. Corroborated by DarkReading/BleepingComputer on the Safari-page-load exploit vector. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/darksword-iphone-exploit-spies-thieves • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-darksword-ios-exploit-used-in-infostealer-attack-on-iphones/
ATT&CKT1189 T1203
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security awareness/phishing-simulation platforms proxying users through the same hosting ranges
  • An analyst manually visiting the reported phishing page from a lab browser to validate takedown
  • Hosting IP re-assigned to a legitimate site after infrastructure takedown
  • URL-rewrite / SASE inspection appliances that re-fetch the page on the user's behalf
Suppression filter
| where SrcHostname !has "phish-sim" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the browser actually rendered the page (HTTP 200 in ImWebSession/RemoteUrl) vs a blocked SASE fetch, and identify the user and whether they hold AWS console or Apple ID access. 2) Contain: block the host at the web proxy, reset the user's AWS console + Apple ID credentials and revoke active sessions/tokens, and check for MFA-prompt fatigue on both. 3) Hunt: correlate the same user/device to any of the 13 infrastructure IPs and to subsequent AWS CloudTrail ConsoleLogin / Apple ID sign-ins from unusual geographies within 24h.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari","arc.exe","opera.exe")
| where RemoteIP in (PhishHosts)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc

| where DstIpAddr in (PhishHosts)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Proxy hunt for DarkSword operator Telegram contact channel t.me/YATA0000 AICommand & Control Low
Low-volume, high-precision hunt for any host in the estate reaching the DarkSword operator's recovered Telegram contact channel (t.me/YATA0000), the only direct operator comms channel Censys recovered from the 亚太集团 (Asia-Pacific Group) C2 Control Panel. A hit indicates either operator activity from inside the estate or a device negotiating an out-of-band exfil/comms path. Rationale: Uses the exact operator contact string hxxps://t[.]me/YATA0000 that Censys rendered from the 亚太集团 C2 Control Panel — the single direct operator channel recovered. Near-zero legitimate traffic to this specific Telegram path makes it a high-precision (if low-volume) hunt; Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty as they lack full-URL-path proxy telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/chinese-threat-actor-uses-leaked.html
ATT&CKT1567 T1102
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel analyst clicking the reported Telegram link during research
  • Automated URL detonation/sandbox following the IOC
  • A Telegram deep-link that legitimately resolves the same handle after the channel is repurposed
  • URL-preview/link-unfurl services in chat apps fetching the link
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host/user and the process that generated the request (browser vs script/tool) and whether it was analyst research. 2) Contain: if non-research, isolate the host and block t.me/YATA0000 plus the associated C2 IP 103.106.190.217 at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot the same host across the 13 DarkSword infrastructure IPs and review for prior watering-hole browser sessions and credential-exfil egress.

| where RemoteUrl has "YATA0000" or RemoteUrl has_all ("t.me","YATA0000")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "YATA0000"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstIpAddr, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-08-03 10 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Non-Chrome process reads Google Password Manager synced-passkey store (Sync Data\LevelDB)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Chrome access to Chrome passkey enclave/device-key material (passkey_enclave_state) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Non-Chrome process reads Google Password Manager synced-passkey store (Sync Data\LevelDB) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the Pass-ta-key Stage-Zero reconnaissance: malware on the endpoint opening/copying Chrome's synced-passkey LevelDB (WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records) to enumerate which relying parties the victim uses passkeys for, plus usernames, credential IDs and encrypted private keys. Access requires no elevation, so any process other than chrome.exe touching this exact path is high-signal. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim path %LocalAppData%\Google\Chrome\User Data\<Profile>\Sync Data\LevelDB and the WebauthnCredentialSpecifics record store named in the article; any non-chrome.exe reader of this specific passkey DB is the enumeration step common to all three Pass-ta-key variants. Cross-checked The Hacker News write-up and Unit42 Part 2. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/
ATT&CKT1217 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup agents (Veeam Agent, Acronis, CrashPlan) snapshotting the Chrome profile directory
  • AV/EDR on-access scanners reading the LevelDB files (MsMpEng.exe, MsSense.exe)
  • Windows Search indexer touching the profile (SearchIndexer.exe / SearchProtocolHost.exe)
  • IT profile-migration or roaming-profile scripts (robocopy/PowerShell Copy-Item) that copy the whole User Data folder to a new machine
  • Browser-data migration utilities when a user moves to a new PC
Suppression filter
| where Actor !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","veeam.agent.exe","anvfsm.sys","agent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the Actor process (image path, signer, hash) and its parent; a signed backup/AV/indexer under services.exe is likely benign, an unsigned binary from Temp/AppData or a LOLBin (robocopy, esentutl, powershell) copying the store is not. Confirm the file scope was the passkey LevelDB, not just the whole profile. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill and quarantine the offending binary, and force-revoke the user's Google session + re-enroll passkeys (treat all synced passkeys on that account as compromised). 3) Hunt: pivot on the Actor hash across the fleet, look for the same process also touching passkey_enclave_state / Local State, and check for subsequent outbound connections to Google enclave/sync endpoints from the non-Chrome process.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data" and ProcessCommandLine has @"Sync Data\LevelDB"
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe" and FileName !~ "chrome.exe"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="cmdline", Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, ActorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Child=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, Path=ProcessCommandLine ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data" and FolderPath has @"Sync Data\LevelDB"
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="filewrite", Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, ActorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Child=FileName, ChildCmd="", Path=FolderPath )
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where Actor !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe")
| order by Timestamp desc
union
( SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where CommandLine has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data" and CommandLine has "Sync Data\\LevelDB"
  | where NewProcessName !endswith "\\chrome.exe"
  | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, User=SubjectUserName, Actor=NewProcessName, Cmd=CommandLine, Parent=ParentProcessName ),
( Event
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 11
  | where EventData has "Sync Data\\LevelDB" and EventData has "Chrome\\User Data"
  | where EventData !has "chrome.exe"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, User="", Actor="sysmon-filecreate", Cmd=EventData, Parent="" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Chrome Process Referencing Google Password Manager Passkey Sync Store
id: 5b1f9d2a-3c47-4e88-9a21-7e6c0f4d1a92
description: Detects a process other than chrome.exe whose command line references Chrome's synced-passkey LevelDB store, indicating passkey enumeration/theft (Unit42 Pass-ta-key).
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:
  - attack.t1217
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '\Google\Chrome\User Data'
      - 'Sync Data\LevelDB'
  filter_chrome:
    Image|endswith: '\chrome.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_chrome
level: high
source:windows.sysmon (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:11) (@CommandLine:*User?Data*Sync?Data\\LevelDB* OR @TargetFilename:*Sync?Data\\LevelDB*) NOT @Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| TargetFileName=/\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\.*\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\/i
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\chrome\.exe$/i
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(MsMpEng|MsSense|SearchIndexer|SearchProtocolHost|GoogleUpdate)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data*Sync Data\\LevelDB*" AND NOT Filesystem.process_name="chrome.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where NOT process_name IN ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Non-Chrome access to Chrome passkey enclave/device-key material (passkey_enclave_state) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Silver/Golden Pass-ta-key key-extraction stage: a process other than chrome.exe reading or copying Chrome's local passkey enclave state (passkey_enclave_state, holding wrapped_identity_private_key / the wrapped Security Domain Secret used to decrypt synced passkey private keys). Unlike the LevelDB enumeration, these device-key files are essentially never touched by anything but Chrome, making this very low-FP. Rationale: Targets the article's named local key-state artifacts (passkey_enclave_state holding wrapped_identity_private_key and the wrapped Security Domain Secret) recovered from the full Unit42 article; these files are decrypted/used only by Chrome's enclave, so a non-chrome reader is the Silver/Golden Pass-ta-key private-key theft. Corroborated via the Unit42 primary source and The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chrome updater / repair components (GoogleUpdate.exe, elevation_service.exe) rewriting enclave state during version upgrades
  • Backup agents (Veeam Agent, Acronis) including the profile in a full-disk snapshot
  • AV/EDR on-access scanning the newly written enclave state file
  • DLP agents fingerprinting files under the Chrome profile
  • Roaming-profile / user-migration tooling copying the entire User Data folder to a new device
Suppression filter
| where Actor !in~ ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe","veeam.agent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the Actor process image, signer and hash; Chrome's own elevation_service.exe/GoogleUpdate.exe are expected, an unsigned or Temp/AppData-launched binary reading passkey_enclave_state is a confirmed key-theft attempt. Check if the same process also read Sync Data\LevelDB (UC1) — the combination is the full Pass-ta-key chain. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the binary, and immediately revoke the Google account's device trust and re-enroll all synced passkeys — assume the Security Domain Secret and every synced private key are exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the Actor hash, look for NCrypt* TPM key export activity (Microsoft-Windows-Crypto-NCrypt operational log) and for non-Chrome outbound sessions to Google cloud-authenticator/sync endpoints from the same host.
union
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FileName in~ ("passkey_enclave_state","wrapped_identity_private_key")
  | where FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data"
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, ActorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Target=FolderPath, File=FileName ),
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("passkey_enclave_state","wrapped_identity_private_key")
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe" and FileName !~ "chrome.exe"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, ActorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Target=ProcessCommandLine, File=FileName )
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where Actor !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","elevation_service.exe")
| order by Timestamp desc
union
( SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where CommandLine has_any ("passkey_enclave_state","wrapped_identity_private_key")
  | where NewProcessName !endswith "\\chrome.exe"
  | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, User=SubjectUserName, Actor=NewProcessName, Cmd=CommandLine ),
( Event
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 11
  | where EventData has_any ("passkey_enclave_state","wrapped_identity_private_key")
  | where EventData !has "chrome.exe"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, User="", Actor="sysmon-filecreate", Cmd=EventData )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

PNLD Breach Exposes U.K. Police and Government Contact Details on Dark Web

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Police National Legal Database (PNLD) has confirmed that police, government and customer contact information was compromised and published on the dark web. The data included names, organisations and work email addresses belonging to police officers, police staff, criminal justice professionals, government partners and customers. The incident, identified on July 26, also exposed some names

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Dataverse table enumeration across Power Pages /_api and /_odata entity sets
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound phishing leveraging the PNLD / ExfilSquad breach against named officers · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anonymous bulk Dataverse extraction via Power Pages Web API / legacy OData feed · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Anonymous bulk Dataverse extraction via Power Pages Web API / legacy OData feed AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts high-volume, successful requests to Microsoft Power Pages Web API ('/_api/') and legacy OData ('/_odata') routes from a single external source — the exact extraction path ExfilSquad used against misconfigured Anonymous Users web roles to pull Dataverse records (names, orgs, work emails) behind the PNLD breach. Surfaces bulk record pulls that a normal portal-browsing session would never generate. Rationale: Anchors on the concrete '/_api/', '/_odata' and '/_services/' Power Pages routes plus a 200-status + high-volume shape confirmed by VenariX and Microsoft Learn as the ExfilSquad extraction path; Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because Power Pages/Dataverse HTTP request logs are not shipped to endpoint EDR or AWS telemetry — the signal lives only in web-tier logs. Cross-checked VenariX, Microsoft Power Platform governance blog, and Microsoft Learn Web API overview. Cross-checked against: • https://venarix.com/blog/exfilsquad-targets-misconfigured-microsoft-power-pages-portals • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-pages/configure/web-api-overview • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/blog/power-pages/governance-control-to-disable-anonymous-access-to-dataverse-data-in-power-pages-websites/ • https://appomni.com/ao-labs/microsoft-power-pages-data-exposure-reviewed/
ATT&CKT1213 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized integration/service accounts (Power Automate, ETL) syncing Dataverse through the portal Web API
  • Portal client-side JavaScript issuing many /_api/ calls to render list/grid views in one legitimate session
  • Approved uptime/synthetic monitors (UptimeRobot, Azure Traffic Manager Endpoint Monitor) polling portal pages
  • Search-engine crawlers (Googlebot, bingbot) indexing portal content
  • Your own authorized web/pentest scan of the portal
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Googlebot","bingbot","UptimeRobot","Azure Traffic Manager Endpoint Monitor","PowerAutomate","Microsoft-Flow")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull SampleUrls for the top SrcIpAddr — identify which Dataverse entity sets were read and whether they hold PII (contacts, systemusers, incidents). Geolocate the IP and check if the UA/IP maps to a known integration. 2) CONTAIN: In Power Platform admin, enable the tenant governance control to block unauthenticated Dataverse reads and remove Anonymous Users table permissions / disable the Web API + legacy OData feed on the affected site; validate access from an unauthenticated browser session. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every Power Pages site in the tenant, test each /_api and /_odata route unauthenticated, and review web logs for the same SrcIpAddr/UA hitting other portals.
let lookback = 24h;
let extractionThreshold = 100;   // 100 = bulk-pull floor; a single interactive portal session rarely hits >100 successful /_api calls
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Url contains "/_api/" or Url contains "/_odata" or Url contains "/_services/"   // Power Pages Web API + legacy OData feed routes
| extend Status = coalesce(HttpStatusCode, HttpResponseCode)
| where Status == 200
| summarize Requests = count(),
            DistinctUrls = dcount(Url),
            TotalRespBytes = sum(HttpResponseBodyBytes),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 15)
    by SrcIpAddr, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| where Requests > extractionThreshold
| order by Requests desc
title: Anonymous Bulk Access to Power Pages Web API / OData Dataverse Endpoints
id: 3f2a1c9e-8b47-4d6a-bf21-7c9e5a1d2b30
status: experimental
description: Detects requests to Microsoft Power Pages Web API (/_api/) or legacy OData (/_odata) routes that expose Dataverse table data, as abused by ExfilSquad against misconfigured Anonymous Users web roles (PNLD and related breaches).

WEB
